questions.question: Before prescribing a topical medication for a rash, what should the FNP establish first?
choices: The patient’s preferred tube size
Lesion morphology, distribution, time course, exposures, and systemic symptoms
Whether the rash is inconvenient
Whether a family member has used the same medication
questions.explanation: Medication selection depends on a defensible diagnosis. Morphology, distribution, timeline, exposures, and red flags help distinguish inflammatory disease, infection, drug reactions, and emergencies.

questions.question: Why must topical corticosteroid potency and duration be chosen carefully?
choices: Topical agents cannot have adverse effects
Higher-risk use can cause skin atrophy and other local or systemic adverse effects
Every rash improves with high-potency steroid
Body site does not affect absorption
questions.explanation: Topical corticosteroids are effective but can cause adverse effects, especially with prolonged/high-potency use or use on thin/high-absorption skin.

questions.question: Which finding in a patient thought to have eczema should prompt reassessment for infection or another diagnosis?
choices: Rapidly worsening pain, warmth, drainage, and fever
Stable itching improved with moisturizer
A chronic unchanged dry patch
Improved sleep
questions.explanation: Pain, warmth, drainage, and systemic symptoms can indicate skin infection or another process rather than an uncomplicated inflammatory flare.

questions.question: What is a key antibiotic-stewardship principle in acne care?
choices: Use oral antibiotics indefinitely as monotherapy
Combine appropriate therapies and limit antibiotic exposure; use benzoyl peroxide with antibiotics when appropriate
Avoid topical therapy in all patients
Refill antibiotics without reassessment
questions.explanation: Acne care benefits from multiple mechanisms. Guidelines emphasize limiting systemic antibiotic use and combining antibiotic therapy with benzoyl peroxide and other topical treatment when appropriate.

questions.question: Which acne presentation merits consideration of dermatology referral?
choices: Severe nodular acne with scarring risk or failure of a structured treatment plan
A single resolved comedone
A patient who uses moisturizer
A normal skin examination
questions.explanation: Severe, scarring, refractory, or diagnostically uncertain acne may require specialist treatment and medication-specific safety programs.

questions.question: What is an important distinction when evaluating a suspected bacterial skin infection?
choices: Whether it is purulent/abscess-associated or nonpurulent cellulitis
Whether the patient likes oral medications
Whether every infection needs a culture
Whether all erythema is cellulitis
questions.explanation: Purulent infection may need drainage, while nonpurulent cellulitis has a different evaluation and empiric-treatment approach. Cellulitis also has important mimics.

questions.question: Which cellulitis finding requires emergency evaluation?
choices: Rapid progression with severe pain out of proportion, systemic toxicity, or altered mental status
Mild stable redness without pain
A healed abrasion
Itching improved by elevation
questions.explanation: Rapid progression, pain out of proportion, systemic toxicity, necrosis, or altered mental status may indicate serious infection and cannot be safely managed by routine outpatient treatment alone.

questions.question: Why can topical steroid treatment be problematic in undiagnosed tinea?
choices: It always cures fungal infection
It may suppress visible inflammation while allowing fungal disease to persist or spread
Fungal disease never itches
It improves diagnostic accuracy
questions.explanation: Steroids can alter the appearance of fungal disease and delay correct treatment. Reconsider the diagnosis when morphology suggests tinea.

questions.question: Which drug-eruption pattern is most concerning?
choices: A new widespread rash with fever, skin pain, blistering, or mucosal involvement
A stable freckle since childhood
Mild dry skin in winter
An old scar
questions.explanation: Fever, skin pain, blistering, mucosal lesions, facial edema, or systemic illness after medication exposure may signal a severe cutaneous adverse reaction and needs urgent assessment.

questions.question: What should be included in follow-up for outpatient cellulitis?
choices: Only whether the patient started the antibiotic
Vital signs/systemic findings, change in spread, clear return precautions, and planned reassessment
No follow-up if redness remains unchanged
A higher antibiotic dose without reassessment
questions.explanation: Documentation, reassessment, and return precautions are essential because cellulitis can worsen, mimic another condition, or require procedural/emergency care.
